This course teaches four products that a careful beginner can make well in a home kitchen: **whipped shea butter**, **body oils**, **hair and scalp oils**, and **simple balms** made with beeswax. All four have one thing in common: they contain **no water**. Makers call these products **anhydrous**, which simply means water-free.
A pump bottle of body product
Lotions look simple, but because they contain water they need a proper preservative, which is why we start with water-free products.
Why water changes everything

Bacteria, yeast and mould need water to grow. A jar of pure shea butter or a bottle of oil gives them almost nothing to live on, so oil-only products do not need a preservative to stay safe from germs. Their main enemy is **rancidity**: oils slowly react with air, light and heat and begin to smell like old groundnuts or crayons. You slow that with fresh ingredients, clean dry containers, and storage away from sun.

A lotion or cream is different. It is a mix of oil and water held together by an emulsifier. The moment water is present, germs can grow, often without any smell or colour change you can see. Formulation teachers such as Humblebee & Me state plainly that anything containing water needs a **broad-spectrum preservative** unless it is used up immediately. That includes products made with aloe vera juice, rose water (a hydrosol), milk or herbal teas. Module 3 explains this fully. For now, the rule is simple: if it has water in it, it needs a real preservative and proper training.

Every product in this course is built from three families of ingredients: **butters** (solid at room temperature), **liquid oils**, and **waxes**. Once you understand what each family does, you can design a formula on purpose instead of copying a recipe you do not understand.
A coconut
Coconut oil is a common local base oil; it turns solid when the weather is cool.
Butters: the body of the product

**Shea butter** is the star. It is soft, rich and melts close to skin temperature, so it spreads easily and leaves a protective feel. Unrefined shea is ivory to yellowish with a nutty, smoky smell. Refined shea is whiter with little smell. Both work; unrefined keeps more of its natural character. **Cocoa butter** is much harder and has a chocolate smell; a little of it makes balms firmer. Mango butter is another soft butter, but it is usually imported and costs more.
Liquid oils: light, medium and heavy

Oils feel very different on skin and hair. A **light** oil sinks in quickly and leaves little shine. A **heavy** oil is thick, stays on the surface longer and feels greasier. Good formulas usually blend one heavier oil with one or two lighter ones.

Waxes: the structure

**Beeswax** turns oils into a solid balm. It melts at roughly 62 to 64 °C, much higher than shea, so balms made with it stay firm in the heat. More wax makes a harder balm; less wax makes a softer salve. Beeswax is an animal product, so it is not vegan; candelilla wax is a plant alternative but harder to find.

Skin needs versus hair needs

Skin and hair need different things. Dry skin likes richer butters that leave a protective layer. A scalp, which has many oil glands and follicles, usually prefers lighter oils that do not sit as a heavy coat. The lengths and ends of tightly coiled hair, which dry out easily, often enjoy heavier oils and butters to seal in moisture after water or a water-based leave-in has been applied. This is the idea behind the "sealing" step many people with natural hair use.

Be honest about what oils do. Oils soften, add shine, reduce friction when combing and help slow moisture loss. They do not feed hair from the outside, and there is no strong proof that any home oil blend makes hair grow faster. You will hear claims about castor oil and rosemary oil for growth. Treat them as popular beliefs, not promises.

Two habits separate a professional maker from a hobbyist: **clean work** and **measured strength**. This lesson covers both. Even water-free products can pick up germs if water or dirty fingers get in, and essential oils can burn or sensitise skin if they are used too strong.
A pair of protective gloves
Gloves and clean tools keep your hands and germs out of the product.
Setting up a clean workspace
Clear the table of food, pets and children. Tie back hair and wear an apron.
Wash the table, then wipe it with 70% alcohol (isopropyl or ethanol) and let it dry.
Wash bowls, spatulas, whisks and jars with hot soapy water, rinse well and dry completely.
Spray or wipe tools and the inside of jars with 70% alcohol and let them air-dry fully before use. The alcohol must evaporate; it should not be wet when you fill.
Wear clean gloves and do not touch your face or phone while working.
Keep a dedicated set of tools for products only, not for cooking.

**Dry is as important as clean.** A single drop of water left in a jar gives germs a place to start. Customers also add water when they dip wet fingers into a jar in the bathroom, which is why it helps to give a small spatula or recommend clean dry hands.

What essential oils are

Essential oils are very concentrated aromatic extracts from plants, usually made by steam distillation or, for citrus peels, by pressing. A small bottle can represent a large amount of plant material. They are not the same as carrier oils such as olive or coconut, which are gentle fatty oils. Essential oils must always be diluted in a carrier before they touch skin.
Safe dilution ranges

The Tisserand Institute, founded by essential oil safety author Robert Tisserand, publishes dilution guidance used widely by aromatherapists. Its general ranges are below. Stay at the lower end when you are not sure, and remember that a nice smell does not need high strength.

For scalp oils, which sit on the skin for hours and are used often, this course takes a cautious approach and stays at 1% or below. For products meant for babies and young children, leave essential oils out completely unless you are following a specialist source; unscented products are a strong selling point for mothers anyway. Advise pregnant customers to check with their health worker before using scented products.
Calculating by weight

Dilution means the percentage of the total product weight. The easiest and most accurate way is to weigh with a small digital scale that reads to 0.01 g (often sold as a jewellery or pocket scale). Drops are a rough backup only: the Tisserand Institute notes that drop conversions are always approximate because drop size varies by oil and bottle.
Worked example: 2% lavender in a body butter
For example, Funke in Ibadan is making 250 g of whipped shea butter for adult body use and wants a light lavender scent.
She chooses 2%, inside the 1 to 3% body range.
Essential oil needed: 250 g x 2 / 100 = 5 g.
The other 245 g is her butter and oil blend.
She places the bowl on the scale, presses tare (zero), and adds lavender drop by drop until the scale shows 5.00 g.
She records "Lavender 5 g, 2%" on her batch sheet.
Her butter is pleasantly scented and within the recognised body range. If she later made a face balm of the same size, 1% would mean only 2.5 g.
Oils that need extra care
**Tea tree, peppermint, cinnamon, clove, oregano and thyme** are known skin irritants. Never use them undiluted and keep them at low levels.

**Cold-pressed citrus oils** such as lemon, lime and bergamot can cause phototoxic burns on sunny skin. IFRA (the fragrance industry standards body) sets a 2% maximum for cold-pressed lemon in leave-on products. For products used in our sun, choose steam-distilled versions or other oils.
**Old, oxidised oils** irritate more. Keep bottles tightly closed, cool and dark, and note the opening date.
Keep peppermint and eucalyptus away from the faces of babies and small children.
Allergy can be permanent

Using essential oils too strong can cause allergic contact dermatitis. Once a person becomes allergic to an oil, they are likely to react to it every time afterwards. Low, measured dilution protects your customers and your name.

Finally, label your bottles, store all oils out of reach of children, and never let anyone swallow essential oils. A small child drinking a bottle is a medical emergency; take them to a hospital immediately with the bottle.

Whipped shea butter is often the first product a natural maker sells, and also the one that shows quality most clearly. Good whipped butter is light, smooth, holds its shape in the jar and melts easily on skin. Poor whipped butter is gritty, collapses into a greasy puddle, or smells stale. The difference is method, not secret ingredients.

Write the formula in percentages first

Professionals write formulas as percentages of the total weight, then convert to grams for each batch size. That way you can make 200 g or 2 kg and the product stays the same. A simple, reliable whipped butter is about **70% shea butter and 30% liquid oil**, with essential oil (if any) taking a small part of the oil share.

More liquid oil gives a softer, more greasy-feeling butter that may slump in hot weather. Less liquid oil gives a stiffer butter. In very hot places or seasons, reduce the liquid oil a little; during harmattan, when coconut oil hardens, you may increase it slightly. Change one thing at a time and record it.
Why shea butter goes grainy

Shea butter contains several different fats that melt and set at different temperatures. If melted shea cools slowly, or is heated and cooled again and again (for example, sitting in a hot shop by day and a cool room at night), some of those fats set first and form small hard crystals. Customers feel these as grains or little lumps that melt on the skin. They are not dirt and not dangerous, but they make your product look poorly made.

The common fix used by formulators is **tempering**: melt the butter completely, keep it fully melted for a while so every crystal disappears, then cool it **quickly** so all the fats set together in a fine, smooth structure.

Fully melting and then cooling quickly is what prevents graininess.
The method
Clean and sanitise your workspace and tools, then let them dry (Module 1, Lesson 3).
Weigh the shea butter and coconut oil into a heat-safe bowl.

Melt over a pot of gently simmering water (a double boiler). Keep the heat low; shea should never smoke or boil. Stir until there are no solid bits at all, then keep it melted for about 10 more minutes while stirring.
Take the bowl off the heat and add the olive oil.

Cool quickly: set the bowl in a larger bowl of cold water with some ice, or place it in the fridge, stirring every few minutes. Stop when the edges are firm and the middle is like soft custard or thick pap.
Add the weighed essential oil now, when the butter is cool, so less scent evaporates.
Whip with a hand mixer for 5 to 10 minutes, scraping the sides, until the butter is pale, light and holds soft peaks. If it stays soft, chill for 10 minutes and whip again.
Spoon or pipe into clean, dry jars, tap to remove air pockets, close and label with the batch number and date.
Worked example: rescuing a grainy batch
For example, Bisi in Lagos made 1 kg of whipped butter. After two weeks in her shop by a sunny window, customers said it felt sandy.
She takes back the unsold jars and checks the batch record: she had cooled the first batch slowly overnight at room temperature.
She scoops the butter into a bowl, melts it fully over low heat and holds it melted for 10 minutes.
She cools it in a bowl of iced water, stirring, then whips it again.
She moves her display stock away from the window and adds "Store in a cool place" to her label.
The rewhipped butter is smooth again. Bisi changes her method sheet so every batch is cooled quickly, and her complaints stop.
Heat safety

Melted oils can cause serious burns and can catch fire if overheated. Use low heat, never leave the pot, keep children away, and keep a lid nearby to cover a pan if oil ever catches fire. Never pour water on burning oil.
Storing and shelf life
Use clean, dry jars with tight lids. Plastic PET jars are light and unbreakable; glass looks premium but can break in transit.
Store away from sun and heat. Whipped butter can melt and lose its fluff above about 30 °C, then set back dense or grainy.
Fresh oils give longer life. Vitamin E (tocopherol) at around 0.5% is often added as an **antioxidant** to slow rancidity. It is not a preservative and does not stop germs.
Set a best-before date you can defend. Use the earliest expiry date of your raw oils as a limit, and track how your own batches smell over time.

Beeswax balms

A balm is oil made solid with wax. A common starting point is **about 1 part beeswax to 4 parts oils and butters by weight** (20% wax). That gives a firm balm suitable for lips and hot weather. For a softer salve for heels or dry patches, try 15% wax. For a stick in a tube, try 25%.
Weigh beeswax, shea and liquid oil into a heat-safe jug. For 100 g: 20 g beeswax, 30 g shea butter, 50 g olive oil.
Melt over a double boiler on low heat. Beeswax needs roughly 62 to 64 °C to melt, so it takes longer than shea. Stir until clear.
Test firmness: dip a cold metal spoon in, let it set for a minute, and press it. Too hard: add a little oil. Too soft: add a little wax. Record any change.
Remove from heat, cool slightly, and stir in essential oil at the correct dilution (lip balms: keep low, and avoid cinnamon, clove and citrus oils on lips).
Pour into clean, dry tins or tubes. Leave undisturbed to set fully before closing.
Packaging matters

Use amber or opaque bottles to protect oils from light. Droppers and small spouts let customers take a little at a time without touching the oil. Make sure caps seal well so oils do not leak in transit or a hot bag.
Checking each finished product
Smell: fresh and pleasant, no sharp or stale note.
Look: clear oils with no cloudiness or bits; balms smooth with no sweating droplets.
Feel: a few drops on your hand should match the feel you designed for.
Weight: each bottle or tin has at least the amount stated on the label.

Finally, think about how long one bottle lasts a customer. A scalp oil used a few drops at a time twice a week can last two or three months in a 100 ml bottle, which gives the oil time to age. A formula is not finished when it looks nice in the jar. It is finished when it has been tested on real skin and hair, over real time, by more than one person. Testing protects customers and also gives you honest information to describe your product.

Testing on skin before regular use

The American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) advises a simple test before using a new skin care product. Choose a small spot where the product will not be rubbed or washed off, such as the inner arm or the bend of the elbow. Apply the normal amount, **twice a day for 7 to 10 days**. If there is no redness, itching or swelling, the person can go ahead and use it. If a reaction appears, wash the product off gently as soon as possible and do not use it again.
Give each tester a small labelled sample and a printed or WhatsApp copy of these instructions.

Record every result, including reactions, in your batch file.
If someone reacts

Tell the person to stop using the product, wash it off gently and see a health worker or dermatologist if the reaction is severe or does not settle. Do not suggest home remedies on top. Record which batch and which ingredients were involved.

Hair products especially need time. Hair and scalp response is usually judged over several wash days, not one application. Aim for at least **four weeks** and at least **five testers**, including people whose hair is different from yours: for example tightly coiled natural hair, looser curls, relaxed hair, and someone with locs or braids. Quality, preservation, honest claims and NAFDAC

This module covers the things that protect customers and your business: why water-based products need proper preservatives, how to write honest claims and labels, what NAFDAC registration of cosmetics involves, and how batch records let you prove and repeat your quality.
Why water-based lotions need proper preservatives
Explain why water lets germs grow in cosmetics
Tell the difference between an antioxidant and a preservative
Identify hidden water in a formula
Decide when a product needs a preservative and what that involves

Many new makers want to sell lotions and creams because customers like their light feel. This lesson explains why that step needs more than a recipe from social media. Even if you never make a lotion, you need to understand this so you can answer customers and avoid copying unsafe products.
A laboratory petri dish
Germs that grow in water-based products are usually invisible until it is too late, which is why preservatives are tested in laboratories.
Water is food and home for germs

Bacteria, yeasts and moulds are everywhere: on hands, in air, in tap water, on jars. They need water to multiply. In a lotion, which is mostly water, they can multiply into very large numbers within days in warm weather. Often you cannot see, smell or feel the contamination until mould spots appear. By then the product may already have caused skin infections, especially on broken skin, around the eyes, or on babies.

Formulation educators are clear on this point. Humblebee & Me, a widely used formulation teaching site, states that anything containing water needs a **broad-spectrum preservative** (one that works against bacteria, yeasts and moulds) unless it will be used immediately, and that an unpreserved water-based product lasts only a few days even in a fridge.
Hidden water
Water is not only the water you pour from a bottle. These ingredients also bring water into a product:
Aloe vera juice or gel
Rose water, orange flower water and other hydrosols
Herbal teas and infusions made in water
Milk, yoghurt, honey mixed with water, fruit purees
Glycerin mixed with water, or any "water phase" in a recipe

A product can also gain water during use. A jar of body butter kept in the bathroom and dipped into with wet fingers slowly gets water inside. That is why the same source notes that anhydrous products used around water may also benefit from a preservative, and why you should advise customers to use dry hands or a spatula.
Antioxidant versus preservative
Antioxidant
Preservative
Slows oils going rancid
Example: vitamin E, rosemary extract
Does not stop germs
Useful in all oil products
Stops bacteria, yeast, mould
Must be broad-spectrum
Needed whenever water is present
Used at the supplier's stated rate
Both are useful, but only a preservative protects a water-based product from germs.

Temperature makes this worse in our climate. Most of Nigeria is warm all year, and warmth speeds up the growth of many germs, so a lotion that might last a little longer in a cold country can spoil faster here.
Things that are not preservatives

Many sellers in markets and online call the following "natural preservatives". According to Humblebee & Me, vitamin E, grapefruit seed extract, rosemary antioxidant extract and essential oils are antioxidants or fragrance, **not** preservatives. Salt, honey and other "antibacterial" kitchen ingredients also cannot replace a real preservative in a lotion. Putting tea tree oil or vitamin E into a homemade cream and calling it preserved is a common and dangerous mistake.
Worked example: is this product safe to sell?
For example, Grace in Benin City sees a video of a "natural whipped lotion" made from shea butter, aloe vera gel and vitamin E, and wants to sell it.
She lists the ingredients and marks hidden water: aloe vera gel is mostly water.
She checks for a broad-spectrum preservative: there is none. Vitamin E is only an antioxidant.
She asks how long it would last: unpreserved, only days, and customers keep jars for months.
She decides not to sell it. Instead she makes a water-free whipped shea and tells customers to apply it to damp skin for a lighter feel.
Grace avoids selling a product that could grow germs in her customers' homes, and still meets the need for a lighter feel.
If you want to make lotions later
Take a proper course in emulsions from a recognised formulation school or supplier, and practise with small batches for yourself only.
Buy a named broad-spectrum preservative from a reputable cosmetic ingredient supplier, with its technical data sheet.
Follow the usage rate and pH range on that data sheet exactly. Preservatives only work within their stated pH range and dose.
Measure pH with a calibrated meter or proper strips, not guesswork.

Before selling, have the product tested by a laboratory. NAFDAC registration requires a laboratory certificate of analysis, and a preservative challenge test is the recognised way to show a preservative system works.
Do not copy formulas without a preservative

If a recipe online contains any water ingredient and no named broad-spectrum preservative, do not make it for sale. If a customer asks you for a lotion, it is honest to say you only make water-free products until you can make lotions safely.

This is not a reason to be afraid of lotions forever. Large and small manufacturers make safe lotions every day. They do it with tested preservatives, clean production, correct pH and laboratory checks. Water-free products let you build a business now while you learn those skills properly.

Aloe, hydrosols, teas and milk all add water.
Vitamin E, rosemary extract, grapefruit seed extract and essential oils are not preservatives.
Unpreserved water-based products last only days, even in a fridge.
Lotions for sale need a proper preservative, correct pH and laboratory testing.

Your label and your WhatsApp posts are promises. In Nigeria, cosmetics are regulated by the **National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC)**. Honest claims and correct labels protect customers and keep your business on the right side of the regulator.
A product label tag
The label carries your promises; every word on it should be true and checkable.
Cosmetic or medicine? It depends on your words

Regulators look at what you say a product is for. The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) explains this idea clearly: a product's **intended use**, shown by its label, advertising and online claims, decides whether it is a cosmetic or a drug. Its examples of claims that make a product a drug include saying it will **restore hair growth**, change melanin production in the skin, or regenerate cells. Nigeria's rules are separate, but the same principle is a safe guide: once you claim to treat, cure or prevent a condition, you are making a medical claim that needs evidence and approval as a medicine.

Two more words need care. **"Organic"** on its own suggests certified organic farming. Do not use "certified organic" unless your ingredients and product are actually certified by a recognised certification body. You can honestly say "made with natural plant butters and oils". **"Chemical-free"** is never true: water, shea butter and beeswax are all chemicals. It also misleads customers.
Never add banned or medicinal ingredients

Do not add hydroquinone, mercury compounds, steroid creams, antibiotic or antifungal creams, or crushed tablets to a product, even in small amounts. These can cause serious harm, and adding them turns your product into an unregistered medicine.
What your label should show

NAFDAC's registration guidelines say labelling must be informative, accurate and comply with the Agency's Cosmetics Labelling Regulations. Read the current regulations on the NAFDAC website before you print. A cosmetic label commonly includes:

What it is and how to use it, including "for external use only" where relevant
Full ingredient list, ideally using standard (INCI) names such as Butyrospermum Parkii (Shea) Butter
Net content (for example 100 g or 50 ml)
Name and address of the manufacturer
Batch number, date of manufacture and expiry or best-before date
Warnings, such as "patch test before use", "contains nut oil" and "keep out of reach of children"

NAFDAC registration in outline

NAFDAC's Guidelines for the Registration of Cosmetics Made in Nigeria set out the process. In summary, an application is made for each product, online and with documents. The documents listed include evidence of business registration (for micro, small and medium enterprises, a CAC business name is accepted), evidence that the brand name is registered with the Trademarks Registry, a satisfactory inspection or Good Manufacturing Practice certificate, label artwork, and a comprehensive laboratory certificate of analysis. Fees apply. The guideline states a timeline of 120 working days from submission to registration.

A batch record is the written story of one production run: what went in, how much, when, by whom, and how it turned out. It is the backbone of consistent quality and one of the things an inspector expects to see. It also saves you money, because when something goes wrong you can find the cause instead of guessing.
A clipboard with a record sheet
One sheet per batch turns your memory into evidence.
Batch numbers

Use a simple system you can keep forever. A common style is the product code, the date and a run number, for example **WSB-261006-01** for whipped shea butter made on 6 October 2026, first batch of the day. Write the same number on every jar from that batch and on the batch record.

Why keep a retained sample

Keep one small sample from every batch in a cool, dark place. If a customer complains about smell or texture in three months, you compare their jar with your retained sample. If both have changed, the formula or an ingredient is the problem. If only theirs has changed, storage or use (such as wet fingers or a hot car) may be the cause.
Setting a best-before date
You cannot see shelf life; you have to earn it. For water-free products, the oils will eventually go rancid. A careful approach is:
Note the expiry or best-before dates of every oil and butter you use. Your product cannot honestly last longer than its shortest-lived ingredient.
Start with a modest best-before, such as 6 to 12 months from manufacture for oil products made with fresh ingredients, kept cool and dark.
Check your retained samples every month for smell, colour and texture, and record what you find.
Extend the date only when your records show the product is still fine at that age. Shorten it if samples change earlier.
Worked example: tracing a complaint
For example, a customer of Ifeoma in Onitsha sends a voice note saying her hair oil "smells like old groundnut" after two months.
Ifeoma asks for the batch number on the bottle: HO-260710-02.
She opens the batch record: the olive oil came from a new supplier she had not used before.
She smells her retained sample from that batch: it also smells stale, while samples from other batches are fine.
She replaces the customer's bottle, messages the other buyers of that batch, and stops buying from that supplier.
Because of batch records and retained samples, Ifeoma finds the cause in minutes, protects her other customers and keeps the customer's trust.
Storing finished stock
Keep finished products in a cool, dark cupboard or carton, off the floor and away from cooking heat, generators and sunny windows.
Sell the oldest batch first (first in, first out). Write the batch number on the outside of each carton.
Do not leave stock in a parked car or a hot market stall all day; heat melts butters and speeds up rancidity.
Check the outside of jars and bottles for leaks or oily residue before each sale and wipe them clean.
Measuring quality over time
Complaints per 100 units sold, and what they were about.
Repeat buyers: how many customers come back within two or three months.
Batches rejected at the release check, and why.
Returns or replacements given.

Costing and pricing your products
Calculate the ingredient cost of a batch and of one unit
Add packaging, labour and overheads to find the full unit cost

Spot the ingredients that drive your cost and adjust

Many makers price by looking at what others charge. That is useful information, but if you do not know your own cost, you may sell every jar at a loss without noticing. This lesson gives you a simple costing method you can repeat for every product.
A person working with a calculator
A costing sheet tells you the true cost of each jar before you choose a price.
Step 1: cost per gram of each ingredient

Divide the price you paid by the grams you got. If you paid ₦4,000 for 1 kg (1,000 g) of shea butter, the cost is ₦4 per gram. Do this for every ingredient and keep it on your supplier sheet. Update it whenever prices change, which in the current Nigerian market can be often.
Step 2: the four layers of cost
What goes into one unit's price
Profit
Overheads (gas, data, transport)
Labour (your time)
Packaging and label
Ingredients are only the base; a price must cover every layer and still leave profit at the top.
**Ingredients**: grams used x cost per gram, for every ingredient.
**Packaging**: jar or bottle, lid, label, and any box or bag.
**Labour**: your hours, paid at a rate you would accept from someone else. If you do not pay yourself, you cannot hire help later.
**Overheads**: gas or electricity, sanitiser, gloves, paper towels, data for marketing, transport to the market, a share of equipment.
Worked example: costing whipped shea butter
For example, Kemi in Ilorin makes a 500 g batch of lavender whipped shea and fills five jars of about 100 g. Prices are illustrative and approximate; use your own market prices.
Shea butter 350 g at about ₦4 per g = ₦1,400.
Coconut oil 100 g at about ₦6 per g = ₦600. Olive oil 45 g at about ₦10 per g = ₦450.
Lavender essential oil 5 g at about ₦1,200 per g (a 10 g bottle at about ₦12,000) = ₦6,000.
Ingredients total = ₦8,450. Packaging: 5 jars at ₦400 plus 5 labels at ₦100 = ₦2,500.
Overheads (gas, sanitiser, gloves) about ₦800. Labour: 2 hours at ₦1,000 per hour = ₦2,000.
Each jar costs Kemi about ₦2,750 before profit. The essential oil alone is ₦1,200 per jar, nearly half of the cost.
Step 3: setting a price

A common small-business approach is to multiply the full unit cost by a markup that covers profit and leaves room for discounts and wholesale. For example, at 1.8 times, Kemi's price would be about ₦4,950, which she rounds to ₦5,000. Then compare with the market. If similar quality jars sell for ₦3,500, she must lower her cost or explain clearly why hers is worth more.

Also count the cost of the products you give away. Tester samples, gifts to influencers and free replacements are real costs. Put them in your monthly records so that your profit figure is honest, and so you can see whether giving samples actually brings paying customers.

Why water matters
Water-free versus water-based
Water-free
Water-based
Must have a real preservative
This course starts with products that contain no water. Makers call them anhydrous, which means water-free. Germs need water to grow, so oil-only products do not need a preservative against germs.
Their main enemy is rancidity. Oils react with air, light and heat, and start to smell like old groundnuts.
A lotion or cream mixes oil and water. The moment water is present, germs can grow, often without any smell you can notice.
So the rule is simple. If it has water in it, it needs a real preservative and proper training.

Four water-free products
Whipped shea butter: rich moisture, hair butter
Body oil: on damp skin after a bath
Hair and scalp oil: scalp, ends and shine
Simple balm: lips, dry patches, cracked heels
You will make four products. Whipped shea butter, for dry skin and for sealing moisture into natural hair.
Body oil, applied after a bath on damp skin.
Hair and scalp oil, for oiling the scalp, sealing ends and adding shine.
And a simple balm with beeswax, for lips, dry patches and cracked heels.
Never make bleaching creams, or anything with hydroquinone, mercury or steroids.
Three families of ingredients
Shea is soft and rich and melts near skin temperature. Cocoa butter is harder.
Light oils sink in. Heavy oils like castor coat and shine. Blend them.
Beeswax turns oils into a balm. More wax makes it harder.
Every product is built from three families. Butters give body. Shea butter is soft and rich, and melts close to skin temperature. Cocoa butter is much harder.
Liquid oils give spread and softness. A light oil sinks in quickly. A heavy oil like castor is thick and sticky, so use it as a smaller part of a blend.
Wax gives structure. Beeswax melts at roughly 62 to 64 degrees Celsius, so balms stay firm in the heat.
Oils soften and protect hair, but do not promise that any oil makes hair grow.

Clean routine before every batch
Dry is as important as clean. One drop of water lets germs start.
Clear the table of food, pets and children
Wash the surface, wipe with 70% alcohol
Wash tools in hot soapy water, dry fully
Sanitise tools and jars, let them air-dry
Gloves on; tools kept for products only

Wash the table, then wipe it with 70% alcohol and let it dry.
Wash bowls, spatulas and jars with hot soapy water, rinse well, and dry them completely.
Wipe tools and the inside of jars with 70% alcohol, and let them air-dry fully. The alcohol must evaporate before you fill.
Wear clean gloves, and do not touch your face or phone while working. Keep these tools for products only, never for cooking.
A single drop of water left in a jar gives germs a place to start.

Step by step
Smooth whipped shea, 70% shea
Melt fully, hold it melted, then cool fast. That stops grains.
Weigh: 70% shea, 30% liquid oil
Melt fully, then hold melted 10 minutes
Cool fast in iced water to soft custard
Add the weighed essential oil when cool

A reliable starting formula is about 70% shea butter and 30% liquid oil. For a 500 g batch, that is 350 g of shea.
Melt the shea and coconut oil until there are no solid bits at all, then keep it melted for about 10 more minutes, stirring.
Off the heat, add the olive oil. Cool quickly in a bowl of cold water with ice, stirring, until the middle is like soft custard or thick pap.
Add essential oil now, when it is cool, so less scent evaporates.
Whip with a hand mixer for 5 to 10 minutes, until pale and light.
Fill clean, dry jars and label with batch number and date.

Bacteria, yeasts and moulds need water to multiply. In a lotion, they can grow into very large numbers within days in warm weather, often without anything you can see or smell.

Batch records
Trace a complaint by batch
Keep one retained sample from every batch, cool and dark.
Ask for the batch number on the bottle
Open the batch record
Smell your retained sample
Replace, warn other buyers, fix the cause
Give every batch a number, and write it on every jar. Ifeoma's customer said her hair oil smelled like old groundnut after two months. Ifeoma asked for the batch number.
The batch record showed the olive oil came from a new supplier.
Her retained sample from that batch also smelled stale. Samples from other batches were fine.
She replaced the bottle, messaged the other buyers of that batch, and stopped using that supplier.
Your best-before date can never be longer than your shortest-lived ingredient. Start modest, and check retained samples every month.

Why this matters
Know your cost before your price

Honest posts bring repeat buyers
Your capstone: one tested hair product
Many makers price by looking at what others charge. If you do not know your own cost, you may sell every jar at a loss without noticing.

And you will finish your capstone: a documented, tested hair product with a 90-day plan.
Costing
The four layers of cost
Ingredients: grams used times cost per gram
Packaging: jar, lid, label
Labour: your hours at a fair rate
Overheads: gas, sanitiser, gloves, data
First, find the cost per gram. If you paid 4,000 naira for 1,000 g of shea butter, it costs 4 naira per gram. Multiply by the grams you use, for every ingredient.
Add packaging: the jar, lid and label.
Add labour. Time a real batch, from setting up to washing up. Labour is the cost new makers most often leave out. If you do not pay yourself, you cannot hire help later.
Add overheads like gas, sanitiser, gloves, data and transport.
Worked example
Costing five jars of whipped shea
For example, Kemi in Ilorin makes a 500 g batch of lavender whipped shea and fills five jars.
Naira prices are approximate.
Packaging: 5 jars and 5 labels
Overheads
Labour: 2 hours
Kemi makes 500 g of lavender whipped shea, five jars of about 100 g.
Her ingredients come to about 8,450 naira. The lavender essential oil alone is 6,000 of that.
Packaging is 2,500 naira.
Overheads are about 800, and 2 hours of labour at 1,000 naira an hour is 2,000.
The full batch costs 13,750 naira. Divided by 5 jars, that is 2,750 naira per jar, before any profit.
Pricing
From cost to price
Never discount below your full unit cost.
Full unit cost times a markup
Compare with the market
Too high? Lower the cost, or explain value
Wholesale: still above full cost
Multiply the full unit cost by a markup. At 1.8 times, Kemi's price is about 4,950 naira, which she rounds to 5,000.
Then compare with the market. If similar jars sell for 3,500, she must lower her cost or explain why hers is worth more.
Her biggest cost is the essential oil. An unscented version costs about 1,550 naira a jar, and many mothers prefer unscented anyway.
A salon needs room for its own profit, so plan a wholesale price, for example around 30% below retail, but still above your full cost.
Recalculate every time ingredient prices change. A price that was profitable three months ago may be a loss today.
Selling honestly
What it is, and the size
What is in it, in plain words
Who it is for
How to use it, with a patch test
Proof: what your testers found
Every post says what the product is, its size, and the main ingredients in plain words.
Say who it is for, like dry skin, heels, or sealing natural hair.
Say how to use it, and patch test before first use.
Then give proof from your own testers. Six testers used it twice a week for four weeks, and most found it light.
Promise softness, shine and moisture, never cures or guaranteed growth. Photograph in daylight with the label readable, and state the price clearly.
Safety first
When a customer reacts
Do not recommend remedies yourself.
Reply quickly; stop use, wash off gently
Severe or spreading: see a health worker
Ask for batch number and photo; record it
Check batch record and retained sample
Refund or replace, then follow up
Even with patch testing, some people will react. Reply quickly and kindly. Ask her to stop using it and wash it off gently.
If the reaction is severe, spreading or not settling, advise her to see a health worker.
Check your batch record and your retained sample.
Offer a refund or a replacement, and follow up a few days later. Never post her photos or complaint without permission.
